_note: The seven BACKING-BAND briefs — a STYLE BOX and an ARRANGEMENT. A band here is a brief for a rhythm section and a horn section that plays BEHIND a soloist: it is not a song, and it is not a solo. What it reserves is SPACE.
_why: Each brief is written for a flugelhorn player who improvises over it. The arrangement is not a backing track for a melody that already exists — it is a set of frames with two reserved windows (the two [Open Trumpet Space: 32 bars] sections) where the soloist plays and the band thins out underneath. Everything else in the brief exists to make those two windows land: a groove that does not move, a harmony that will not resolve, an ensemble that knows when to shut up.
_why-split: TWO FIELDS, because they are two different jobs. The STYLE BOX is global — it governs the whole track, and Suno weights it far more heavily than the lyrics field. The ARRANGEMENT is section-by-section, and it travels in the LYRICS/PROMPT field as square-bracketed section tags (the same split lib/suno-kai-dna.js makes: six movements, clock times, movement titles). Putting the arrangement in the style box would spend the 1000 characters that the timbre needs.
_why-limits: The server's tag limit is 1000 characters and its prompt limit is 5000. MEASURED against these seven: every STYLE here fits the 1000-character tag limit with room to spare (the longest is 468 characters), so nothing needs truncating and nothing needs moving to the exclusions field. The truncation path still exists in the loader (lib/suno-backing-bands.js § styleText) for a hand-added brief: it cuts at a CLAUSE boundary and hands the overflow to the negative field rather than dropping a word mid-sentence.
_why-open-space: THE CONTRACT: exactly TWO [Open Trumpet Space: 32 bars, …] sections per arrangement, and they are the point. One window is too small — the soloist arrives and leaves with no room to settle; three or more stop being an arrangement and become a jam. 32 bars is the shortest window that still holds a complete phrase and a breath. The three [No …] lines close the brief: no lead melody (the band is not the tune), no horn solos (the solo space belongs to the player, not to the generator), no vocals (Suno invents a singer otherwise).
_why-raw: The house aesthetic: imperfection is the point. Every brief here names the defects to KEEP — human swing, imperfect ensemble attacks, natural breathing, dry horn attacks without vibrato, room microphone bleed, analog tape hiss. A backing band that is too polished is a backing band the soloist cannot trust.
_why-vocabulary: No entry names a person. These are briefs for instruments and an ensemble, so there is no subject to describe, and the house rule is that a published pack never carries a demographic claim about a person (AGENTS.md § 'Prompts must not name the subject's race or ethnicity'). The lint in lib/prompt-lint.js is run over every style and every arrangement as part of the test suite. Genre and TRADITION names (Afro-Latin, New Orleans) are musical lineage, not claims about a person, and they are the artist's own wording — carried VERBATIM.

At 72 BPM the 32-bar window is nearly two minutes: hold your own time against the band, not against a click.

bands.note: The broken-beat groove is the risk: Suno tends to straighten a broken beat back into 4/4 as soon as the horns thin out, and this brief asks for exactly that thinning in the first window. The Rhodes vamp is the harmonic anchor and the drums are the time anchor — if the pulse squares up, re-roll before you play. 1950s chamber-jazz horn writing over a modern broken beat is the whole idea; do not let it become either thing alone.
